title: The computer fills in what you meant
statement: The computer understands the purpose of the program and fills in steps that were left out, so a program does what you meant as long as the intention is clear.

evidence_patterns.item_shape: predict the output of a program with a missing step
evidence_patterns.signature: predicts the intended output rather than the literal one

discriminators.vs_slip: Consistent across items and the learner appeals to what the program is 'for'. A slip is a single misread.

vs.prog.var.names-meaningful-to-machine: The variable-name case is a special case; test with an item where the intention is stated only in a comment.

conflicts_with.label: The machine does exactly what the code says

resolved_by.label: The machine does exactly what the code says
Statements run one at a time in order

sources.citation: Pea, R. D. (1986). Language-independent conceptual "bugs" in novice programming. Journal of Educational Computing Research, 2(1), 25-36.

Sorva, J. (2012). Visual Program Simulation in Introductory Programming Education (Doctoral dissertation, Aalto University). Appendix A catalogues introductory programming misconceptions from the literature.
Qian, Y., & Lehman, J. (2017). Students' misconceptions and other difficulties in introductory programming: A literature review. ACM Transactions on Computing Education, 18(1), Article 1.

provenance.notes: Drafted from the cited literature for the OML seed pack; statement, examples and discriminators are original text. Awaiting maintainer review.
